paras: The whitecap attack on Lucius Brownlee was a night shooting in Monroe County, Georgia, in July 1903, in which a band the Tribune called 'whitecaps' fired on Brownlee, a Black man who had testified in federal court in a moonshine case, and ordered him to leave the county. Five Monroe County men were charged in federal court with conspiring to drive him out to prevent his testimony, and all were acquitted at Macon in June 1904.

Brownlee had testified in the federal court at Macon against Thomas W. Gilmore in a moonshine case. According to the Savannah Morning News, the men had been reported for running a still and had traced the government's information to Brownlee.

Several nights before July 27, 1903, Brownlee was called from his bed, and according to a Macon dispatch to the New-York Tribune 'a volley of bullets and buckshot was fired at him.' The next morning he found a note saying that the shooting was only a warning and ordering him to leave the county. The Savannah Morning News described the attackers as 'a crowd' that visited his home, ordered him to leave and fired several shots into the building. Neither report says that Brownlee was hurt.

Deputy Marshal Thomas brought Ossie Clemmons, John Zellner, James Fletcher and 'Jim' Alexander to Macon, where they were placed under heavy bond to be tried for conspiracy and intimidation of United States witnesses. The Savannah Morning News listed Gilmore among those arraigned before the United States commissioner and reported that each man gave a $500 bond at Forsyth.

Gilmore, James Alexander, J. H. Fletcher, Otto Clement and John Tellner were indicted for conspiracy to drive Brownlee from Monroe County to keep him from testifying against Gilmore in an illicit distilling case. Their trial in federal court at Macon lasted two days and ended in acquittal on June 14, 1904. The Savannah Morning News noted that the case drew attention and that a large contingent of Monroe County people attended.

Coverage was brief and treated the attack mainly as a federal-court matter. The New-York Tribune ran a telegraphed Macon dispatch headed 'WHITECAPS SHOT NEGRO', with a deck stressing the charge of 'Intimidating a Government Witness'. In Georgia, the Savannah Morning News reported the bonds in its state column and later headed the verdict 'Held Not Guilty of Conspiracy Against a Negro', without comment. The Birmingham Age-Herald and the Montgomery Advertiser printed the same Macon acquittal dispatch on June 15, 1904.

A syndicated 'Cream of News' summary carried a single unsigned line on the arrests, naming neither Brownlee nor the accused, in the Gainesville Star and in the Black Savannah Tribune. No Black paper in the coverage reported the attack, the trial or the acquittal in its own words.

The Tribune said the shots were fired at Brownlee and the order to leave came in a note, while the Savannah Morning News said the shots went into the house and the order was given in person. The Tribune and the syndicated brief counted four accused men, while the Savannah Morning News and the 1904 trial reports named five, including Gilmore. Only the Savannah Morning News gave races for the accused, calling four of them white and 'Zeiner' a Black man.

bases: A night band the Tribune called 'whitecaps' fired on a Black man at his home and ordered him to leave the county, and the federal charge was conspiracy to drive him out (A1, A3, A5).

The Tribune's Macon dispatch (A1) and the Savannah Morning News's separate report (A3) agree on a night attack with gunfire and an order to leave, and the 1904 trial reports (A5, A6) confirm the federal conspiracy charge over Brownlee.

framing.detail: The Tribune headed its telegraphed dispatch 'WHITECAPS SHOT NEGRO' with the deck 'Four Men Charged with Intimidating a Government Witness'.
The Savannah Morning News ran the arrests as 'Bonds for Conspiracy' in its state column and the verdict as 'Monroe County Men Acquitted at Macon', with no comment on the outcome.
The Gainesville Star and the Montgomery Advertiser carried the syndicated brief and the Macon acquittal dispatch without comment.
The Savannah Tribune printed only the same syndicated 'Cream of News' line on the four Monroe County men, with no comment and no names.

The 1904 indictment as reported names five defendants including Gilmore.
The Macon dispatch dated July 27 is closer to the event than the syndicated summary.
